candidates.speaker: Joe Schmid
candidates.proposition: Trinitarianism and classical divine simplicity form an inconsistent tetrad if divine processions are positive ontological items intrinsic to but distinct from God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The host explicitly turns the discussion over to Joe, who introduces and enumerates the four claims before yielding to Christopher.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The tetrad directly challenges whether classical divine simplicity can coexist coherently with Trinitarian persons and their asymmetric processions.
candidates.contextSummary: After introductory remarks that divine simplicity comprises several distinct debates, Joe opens the selected Trinitarian objection by laying out four jointly inconsistent commitments.

candidates.speaker: Chris Tomaszewski
candidates.proposition: A Latin Trinitarian model preserves divine simplicity by identifying each person and procession with the divine nature while distinguishing persons through opposed relations.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joe explicitly yields to Christopher, and the speaker begins by rejecting the tetrad's first claim before presenting a sustained Latin Trinitarian account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal classical-theist answer to the alleged conflict between divine simplicity and the reality and distinction of the Trinitarian persons.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe's tetrad claiming that Trinitarian processions are positive intrinsic items distinct from God.

candidates.contextSummary: Chris concedes that social Trinitarian models conflict with simplicity, then argues that a Latin relational model avoids treating the persons as parts or additions to God.

candidates.speaker: Joe Schmid
candidates.proposition: The Son's asymmetric begottenness distinguishes the Son from the unbegotten Godhead, yielding an intrinsic item not strictly identical with God and therefore composition.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly frames the passage as a non-classical-theist response and then yields the last word to Christopher by name.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets the crucial relational-identity maneuver by arguing that asymmetric generation reinstates precisely the intrinsic distinction simplicity excludes.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Chris's claim that the persons are relations identical with the divine essence yet distinguished from one another.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of why the Trinity has no strict creaturely analogue, Joe presses the asymmetry between the begotten Son and the unbegotten Godhead against Chris's model.

candidates.speaker: Chris Tomaszewski
candidates.proposition: The Son is identical with his begottenness, while relational directedness distinguishes him from the Father without adding another positive ontological item to the divine essence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joe explicitly gives Christopher the last word, and the response uses first-person formulations to explain the metaphysics of the Son's begottenness.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response directly defends relational identity against the asymmetry objection and explains why begottenness does not introduce composition into God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe's argument that the Son's begottenness makes him intrinsically distinct from the unbegotten Godhead.

candidates.contextSummary: Chris answers that begottenness describes the Son insofar as he is directed toward the Father, whereas the Son considered absolutely is the divine essence itself.

candidates.speaker: Joe Schmid
candidates.proposition: In a possible world where God creates nothing, God's contingent knowledge must be intrinsic, making it a contingent accident in God and contradicting divine simplicity.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joe announces the aloneness argument, develops both its short and extended forms, cites its premises, and explicitly turns the discussion over to Christopher.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly alleges that divine freedom, omniscience, and the absence of accidents cannot jointly coexist with divine simplicity in an uncreated world.
candidates.contextSummary: After closing the Trinitarian exchange, Joe introduces a new aloneness argument: classical theism permits God alone, yet omniscience gives God contingent knowledge in that world.

candidates.speaker: Chris Tomaszewski
candidates.proposition: God's existing alone does not entail that every property God then has is intrinsic, because aloneness itself can change through creation without any intrinsic change in God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks how Chris will respond, and Chris expressly identifies premise two as false before supplying and explaining the aloneness counterexample.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The counterexample attacks the inference on which the aloneness argument depends, namely that nothing can be extrinsic to God in a God-only possible world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe's premise that any positive reality present when God exists alone must be intrinsic to God.

candidates.contextSummary: Chris first situates the objection within the traditional treatment of changing divine knowledge, then argues that relational properties may remain extrinsic even in an alone world.

candidates.speaker: Chris Tomaszewski
candidates.proposition: Knowledge is extrinsic insofar as it entails truth, since a subject can cease knowing when external reality changes even if nothing intrinsic to the subject changes.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same identified speaker explicitly shifts from the aloneness counterexample to knowledge and develops a first-person hypothetical before inviting Joe's response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This factivity argument directly addresses contingent divine knowledge rather than properties generally and offers an independent defeat of the critic's intrinsic-knowledge premise.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joe's claim that God's contingent knowledge in an alone world must constitute contingent intrinsic reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Chris uses a hypothetical lone creature who knows there are no dogs to argue that knowledge depends on externally varying truth and is therefore not wholly intrinsic.
